title: Case Study + Deep Dive: Telemedicine Support Agents with LangGraph/MCP - Dan Mason
talk_summary: Dan Mason describes a LangGraph/MCP telemedicine support agent that replaces humans clicking buttons with an LLM-driven workflow over markdown 'blueprints', gated by a live LLM-as-judge evaluator that scores confidence and complexity to decide when a human must approve. Key transferable mechanisms are the confidence/complexity deduction framework, retry nodes that wipe malformed tool-call messages, compressed state snapshots, and a custom eval harness with an LLM rubric.

takeaways.technique: Confidence+complexity deduction gate before human review
takeaways.what_they_do: A separate evaluator agent scores each proposed action on a confidence framework with explicit deductions (multiple messages, changed patient data, duplicate/reminder errors); anything below a 75% threshold is routed to a human for approve/feedback/defer instead of auto-sending.
takeaways.evidence_quote: in the confidence framework, we say when you have all of these changes at once, you should deduct from your confidence score
takeaways.numbers: threshold 75%; example run scored 70% and was escalated

takeaways.technique: Retry node that deletes malformed tool-call message and re-prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: When an agent emits invalid JSON/tool call or ends its turn silently, a retry node detects it in code, wipes that message from context (to prevent hallucinated results), and sends the agent back with 'you screwed up, try again'.

takeaways.technique: Compressed state snapshot per turn, discard reasoning traces
takeaways.what_they_do: Each patient turn loads a serialized 'schedule document' (messages, anchors, unsent messages) but not the agents' internal reasoning/tool chatter; that is kept only in LangSmith for debugging. State is re-serialized and re-sent fresh each turn rather than accumulated.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're compressing after every one of these interactions into only the changes that happen to the state ... we do not save this in the state on the blue box
takeaways.numbers: avg ~10-15k tokens per turn; most complex conversation ~150 texts

takeaways.technique: Custom eval harness with LLM rubric over recorded states
takeaways.what_they_do: Pulls datasets from LangSmith, pre-processes timestamps so old runs are comparable, replays them against the graph, and scores output state with an LLM-as-judge rubric (PromptFu) that is deliberately fuzzy ('is anything completely busted?') with explicit notes on what to ignore.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I can't put in an eval from three weeks ago and run it now and get equivalent times ... we ended up sort of doing a hybrid of both

takeaways.technique: Human-maintained markdown blueprints with rationale, not RAG
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of RAG, they keep small self-referential markdown docs (overview links to phase files, triage CSV) and give the whole relevant doc to the model; each instruction includes *why* it matters, which they say improves decisions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It's much more helpful to actually give the LLM justification for why it would say something because then it makes better decisions

takeaways.technique: Aggressive prompt caching within a single conversation
takeaways.what_they_do: They cache the system prompt and multi-turn message history explicitly with Claude, keeping one stable agent identity to avoid cache invalidation, and accept higher per-turn token counts because caching offsets it.
